title: Units Technical Reference
readerIntent: Audit unit definitions and conversion contracts.
summary: Every unit has stable identity, dimension, canonical conversion, precision, rounding, lifecycle, localization, and tests.

sections.heading: Authority and model
items: Units owns reusable dimensions, units, symbols, conversion factors, precision, rounding metadata, activation, and stable business codes. It does not own Inventory, Pricing, Product, land, or agriculture rules.
A dimension groups compatible quantities such as count, mass, volume, length, area, or time. Conversion is permitted only inside the same compatible dimension and configured system.
Original value and unit are retained where audit or business meaning requires them; normalized values support comparison, calculation, search, and storage contracts.

sections.heading: Configuration and extension
items: Define canonical units, allowed conversions, scale, rounding mode, display symbol, aliases, locale behavior, and active state through owned schema and properties contracts.
Reuse existing dimensions and units before adding new ones. A partner-specific unit needs an unambiguous definition, conversion evidence, display guidance, migration, and collision check.
Business modules decide which dimensions and units are allowed for each field; Units validates measurement semantics but cannot decide whether a product is sellable.

sections.heading: Runtime contract
items: Callers submit value, source unit, target or canonical unit, required precision, and context. The service rejects unknown, inactive, incompatible, non-finite, or policy-disallowed input.
Conversions use deterministic numeric handling and documented rounding at the correct boundary. Repeated conversion should not accumulate hidden precision loss.
Generated models and services persist definitions through framework database contracts; consumers do not query provider collections directly.

sections.heading: Examples and boundaries
items: Inventory may receive 125 kilograms, sell 750 grams, and normalize both to an approved mass unit while retaining original quantities for movement evidence.

Land inventory may use hectares and square metres; liquid stock may use litres and millilitres. Area cannot convert to mass, and volume-to-mass requires separate domain data rather than a unit shortcut.
Pricing includes the selling unit because a price per kilogram differs from a price per item even when both reference the same product.

sections.heading: Verification and operations
items: Test zero, negative policy, fractional values, maximum scale, rounding boundaries, aliases, inactive units, incompatible dimensions, duplicate codes, localization, import/export, and schema evolution.
Monitor conversion rejection, unknown units, precision loss, and definition changes with safe bounded labels. Changes that reinterpret stored values require governed migration.
Document business setup, developer extension, supported dimensions, calculation rules, limitations, and rollback whenever unit contracts change.

sections.heading: Checklist
items: Code, name, symbol, dimension, active state, canonical unit, factor, offset where supported, scale, precision, and rounding.
Tenant/global ownership, localization, aliases, version compatibility, and deprecation.
Positive, invalid, incompatible-dimension, boundary, precision, round-trip, integration, and regression tests.
